newsitem.title: BURMA: FEATURE - Buddhism, way of life in Burma.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Buddhism, way of life in Burma.

text.p: Minutes after the mid-morning bell tolls at Mahagandhayon Monastery, hundreds of shaven-headed monks -- some as young as seven years -- form an orderly line to receive their main meal of the day.

The monks, barefoot and wearing the traditional dark red robes of their monastery, move quietly into the large dining hall after receiving large portions of rice and other food from women serving from several oversized couldrons.

"This food was made and donated by a family in the village," says Kay Hla Za, a monk who teaches meditation at Mahagandhayon -- one of the nation's best-known and most respected monasteries which is located in this village in central Burma. "Other days we go out in the village to beg for food."

Red, orange or yellow-robed monks carrying alms bowls are a common sight across Burma, but they are especially so on the streets of this village, a satellite of Burma's second city of Mandalay which is home to nearly two-thirds of the nation's monks.
Even the poorest people find some food to give because it is part of the "merit-making" aspect of Theravada Buddhism -- the religion followed by about 85 percent of the population.
According to the tenets of the religion, people can try to reduce the suffering in this life and the next by performing merit-making activities such as feeding monks or making donations to temples.
BUDDHISM PERMEATES BURMESE LIFE
Burma is considered to be one of the most profoundly Buddhist countries in the world, and the religion permeates all walks of life, including politics.
"Buddhism is trying to get away from mundane suffering, and that's what everyone is trying to do here," said one former top army official who used to be a monk.
Monks played a key role in 1988 national pro-democracy uprisings when hundreds of thousands of people took to the streets to protest against the military government.
Prominent monks appeared on television and appealed to the public to stay calm and pursue their cause peacefully while at the same time urging military leaders to listen and not use force.
The demonstrations were eventually quashed by the military in a bloody showdown that left thousands of people -- including monks -- dead or imprisoned.

Since then, monks have been silenced, through fear and in part through offerings given by the generals in the State Law and Order Restoration Council (SLORC). "The monks were warned not to mix in politics," said one former monk. "The older ones were also given privileges, pagodas, televisions and other things to keep them happy and out of politics."
SLORC BUILDS UPON BUDDHIST MENTALITY
The SLORC regularly builds new temples or donates gifts or money to monasteries or monks.

Some analysts say the SLORC, attacked by many western governments and human rights organisations for human rights abuses and its failure to recognise a democraticaly-elected government, has benefited from having a nation of staunch believers.
"There is a lot of patience here," said one diplomat. "It's one thing that may be working in favour of this government."

"They keep showing top officials paying their respects, which helps legitimise the government because people think they are being good Buddhists," he said, noting the government fears a resurgence of support by monks for the democracy movement led by Nobel Peace laureate Aung San Suu Kyi.
CAN MONKS HELP BRING DEMOCRACY TO BURMA?

Suu Kyi, a staunch Buddhist who won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1991 for her non-violent efforts to bring democracy to Burma, also regularly pays respects to the monks with offerings of food and clothes.

The mere presence of a line of monks at an impromptu pro-democracy gathering in Rangoon recently sparked applause from democracy supporters, who feel support of the monks could be crucial for major change to take place.
"Yes, definitely they will play an important role," said the former army officer, noting it may still take some time.
although some monks may be willing to get involved in politics, it is not yet a massive movement. Kay Hla Za at Mahagandhayon Monastery refused to even discuss the topic.

"This is my world. It is almost as if everything outside these gates is in a foreign country to which I do not belong," he said. "Here we meditate to make the mind calm and quiet. We do not get involved."
